name: Kobe
lede: Kobe is a deep brick-brown red from the color charts of the 1920s, and nothing in our books explains its name.

sections.title: A name without a story
sections.body:
Kobe is a deep red-brown. Our library lists it in the ISCC-NBS system as block 40 and in Maerz and Paul's 1930 *Dictionary of Color*, which gives 1924 as the year it was first recorded [1]. The obvious reading is the Japanese port city, but no source we hold says so, and who coined the color name is undocumented [1][2].

The word appears once in the 29 color books, and only as a place: in 1932 the pearl farmer Mikimoto burned 720,000 rival pearls in a bonfire outside the Kobe Chamber of Commerce [2][3]. That is a story about pearls, not about a color.

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: The nearest named colors in our library are [[brick]] and [[burnt-umber]] [1]. In our archive of 23,781 paintings, 869 (3.7 per cent) hold a color within six units of this swatch over at least five per cent of the canvas [4]. It peaks in the 1400s: 117 of 945 works, 3.4 times the archive rate [4]. Its company is the dark reds, [[maroon]] and [[mahogany]] among them [1][4]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so a match is not a pigment test [4].

origin.named_after: origin undocumented (the Japanese port city is the obvious but unsourced guess)

openers: Kobe the color has no documented story: the only book mention of the word is a pearl-burning bonfire in 1932.
